meta.title: Alternative to Mem0, Zep, cognee and OpenViking
meta.description: A fair comparison of ai-memory with Mem0, Zep, cognee, Letta, OpenViking and Claude's own memory: what carries over, what you gain and where they win.

hero.title: Migrating from another memory tool
hero.lede: Every memory tool is built around one bet. This page says what each of them is for, what changes if you move, and where ai-memory is the weaker choice.

families.title: Each tool optimizes one thing
families.lede: ai-memory optimizes a git-backed wiki of markdown pages with a derived search index, and it makes zero LLM calls by default. The others made different bets, for different buyers.

items.title: Fact extractors
items.text: Mem0 and LangMem ask an LLM to pull atomic facts out of every turn, to personalize an app for its end users.

items.title: Temporal graphs
items.text: Zep, Graphiti and cognee model knowledge as a graph over time. They serve graph queries and run on top of a graph database.

items.title: Memory operating systems
items.text: Letta and MemGPT let the agent edit its own tiered memory. They suit people who adopt their agent runtime.

items.title: Hosted APIs
items.text: Supermemory and the managed clouds keep your memory behind an account, in exchange for connectors and zero operations.

unique.title: What no other tool has all of
unique.lede: The project audited its competitors against its own code. Most have one or two of these six, and none has all six.
unique.teamsText: Accounts give you attribution and an audit log. They are not a tenancy boundary: every user on a server sees every project on it. Plan for one team per server.

stack.title: What you have to run
stack.lede: The quickest way to compare memory tools is to count the services each one needs before it remembers anything.
stack.figureAlt: Diagram: a typical memory stack is four services wired to each other, an LLM API, a vector store, a graph database and a Python service. ai-memory is one binary that writes to one markdown folder.
stack.figureCaption: A typical stack against ai-memory. Not every tool needs all four; the table below says which needs what.
stack.caption: Moving parts each memory tool needs
stack.ours: One binary and a folder of markdown
stack.after: Three rows have no marks. Claude Code’s memory is built in, and basic-memory and mcp-memory-service are also light to run. Their differences are in the next section.

tools.title: Tool by tool
tools.lede: Open the one you use. Every block says what stays the same, what you gain, and where that tool wins.
tools.after: The “where it wins” lines come from the project’s own audit. Read the full comparison and the self-critical parity audit on GitHub.

benchmark.title: The benchmark, with its caveats
benchmark.lede: ai-memory publishes one number, measured on LongMemEval-S with a harness that ships in the repository. Systems that rerank score higher.
benchmark.chartLabel: Bar chart of LongMemEval-S hit at 5. {bars}
benchmark.axis: hit@5, from 0 to 1. Solid bars were measured by this project. Hatched bars are the vendors’ own numbers and were not reproduced here.
caveats: hit@5 asks whether a session holding the evidence is in the top five results. It measures retrieval. It says nothing about answer accuracy.
470 of the 500 questions are scored. The 30 abstention questions are excluded. The run is from {date}.
{local} uses the default in-process embedding model, with no API key and no LLM. {fts} is full text, entities and links only.
No head-to-head run against any competitor exists. Accuracy figures such as Hindsight’s 91.4% are a different metric and do not compare with hit@5.
Stored excerpts are capped at 2 KB for privacy, so evidence deep inside one long turn cannot be found. The benchmark measures the shipped system.
LongMemEval is chat-assistant history. A coding-session benchmark is planned and does not exist yet.

behind.title: Where ai-memory is behind
behind.lede: This list comes from the repository’s own audit. If one of these is what you need, stay where you are.

items.title: No local reranker
items.text: Retrieval scores sit below the systems that rerank. The only reranker is an LLM, and it is off by default. Cited answers need an LLM too, and their accuracy has not been evaluated.

items.title: Link types do not move ranking
items.text: You can walk from a page to its related pages. In search, the kind of link still only explains a result and carries no weight.

items.title: Aging features are unproven
items.text: The confidence score, compaction, dedup and the dream pass are off by default. No recall evaluation has been run on them, so the project claims the mechanism and no measured gain.

items.title: One timeline
items.text: Point-in-time search uses the time a fact was recorded. Zep models both when something happened and when it was learned.

items.title: Text from coding sessions only
items.text: It ingests no PDFs, CSVs or images, has no vision model, and is not a graph database you can query with Cypher.

items.title: One server, no hosted tier
items.text: Many machines reach one server that you run. There is no automatic replication, no SaaS and no enterprise console.

items.title: More setup than built-in memory
items.text: Claude Code’s own memory is already on. ai-memory asks a solo developer to start a server first.

move.title: How to move
move.lede: You do not have to switch in one go. Both tools can run on the same project while you compare them.
move.figureAlt: Diagram: git history and the README and docs feed through bootstrap into the ai-memory folder. Your agent connects to ai-memory and to your current memory tool at the same time, and the two are independent.

steps.title: Install it next to what you have
steps.text: ai-memory adds its own MCP entry and its own hooks, and leaves the entries of other tools in place. The quick setup has the commands.

steps.title: Seed the wiki from the project itself
steps.text: ai-memory bootstrap reads your git history, README, docs/ and agent rules files, then writes seed pages. It needs an LLM provider. Run the dry run first to see what would be sent. Review what lands: an LLM can write plausible details that are wrong, and the wiki is in git so you can revert.

steps.title: Bring old notes and conversations, if the importer reads them
steps.text: The standalone importer under companions/ai-memory-importer reads two things today: oh-my-claudecode (OMC) markdown wiki folders, and conversations in a small generic JSON envelope. It has no Mem0, Zep or cognee adapter, so exports from those need converting to the envelope first. It defaults to a dry run and never deletes.
steps.codeTitle: dry run, from a checkout of the repo

steps.title: Run both for a while, then decide
steps.text: Keep the old tool connected while you compare. Ask both the same questions about your project. Remove whichever one you stopped reaching for.

move.after: The importer’s formats and safety rules are in the companion crates guide. Other ways to bring documents in are in the cookbook.

items.q: Do I need an LLM API key?
items.a: No. Capture, search and handoffs work with no key and no LLM. Adding a provider turns on LLM consolidation, bootstrap, richer linting, auto-improve and optional reranking. Subscription logins such as Codex or GitHub Copilot also work as providers.
No. ai-memory is a single server that you run on a laptop, a homelab box or a LAN host. There is no SaaS tier and no enterprise console.

items.q: Can I import my data from Mem0, Zep or cognee?
items.a: Not directly. The companion importer reads oh-my-claudecode markdown wikis and a generic conversation JSON format. Adapters for specific products live outside the repository. For an existing codebase, ai-memory bootstrap seeds the wiki from git history and docs.

items.q: Can I run ai-memory next to my current memory tool?
items.a: Yes. It installs as its own MCP server entry and its own lifecycle hooks, and it leaves other tools’ configuration alone. You can compare both on the same project before removing either.

items.q: How does its retrieval score compare?
items.a: On LongMemEval-S it scores {local} hit@5 with the default local embeddings and {fts} with full text only. That number measures retrieval and says nothing about answer accuracy. Systems that rerank score higher: agentmemory reports 0.952 and mcp-memory-service reports 0.860 at session level.

items.q: Does it sync memory between machines?
items.a: It uses one server that all of your machines reach over the network. There is no automatic replication between servers.
